headline_insight: Female clients return a Net Promoter Score of 19.2 against 10.4 for men — a near nine-point advantage — yet women are also markedly more likely than men to attribute a low score to poor explanation and training (53.8% vs 42.9% of detractor comments), meaning women are simultaneously VisionFund's strongest advocates and the group most exposed to an information gap.
paragraphs: Among the 1,518 female respondents, 45.2% are promoters, 28.9% passives and 26.0% detractors, producing a Net Promoter Score of 19.2. The 586 male respondents score lower on every dimension of advocacy: 40.6% promoters, 30.2% detractors and an NPS of 10.4. Both subgroups are large enough to be treated as robust. The gender gap in advocacy is not, however, mirrored in the underlying attitudinal measures: 72.4% of women and 75.4% of men say the cover is 'definitely worth it' (a 3.0-point difference that is not statistically significant, p_adj 0.4), and 71.4% of women against 70.3% of men are 'very confident' a claim would be paid (also not significant). In other words, women and men value the product and trust the payout promise at essentially the same rate; what differs is women's willingness to actively recommend it. Households reporting a member with a disability show a weaker picture — NPS of 9.2 (n=477) versus 19.1 for households without (n=1,621), driven by a higher detractor share of 32.3% against 25.6%. No external benchmark data is available for NPS on this indicator, so these figures should be read against each other rather than against any industry norm.

The qualitative evidence explains the tension the numbers leave open, and it is worth naming the divergence directly rather than reading NPS as a single undifferentiated score. The dominant reason clients give for a low score and the dominant reason they give for a high score are two faces of the same variable: whether the product has been understood and experienced. Half of all detractor comments (288 mentions, 50.4%) concern education and training, and this theme is skewed female (53.8% of women's detractor comments versus 42.9% of men's, a 10.9-point gap). A female client in Malawi was explicit about where the failure sits: "We did not understand the claim insurance processes, the officer focused more on loans, and the insurance was not well explained. We need special training of insurance for us to understand." Another female client in Malawi described the resulting ambivalence — she had heard positive feedback from others but personally struggled "to see its necessity... the cost of maintaining the insurance feels difficult to justify, especially when the benefits are not clearly visible." On the promoter side, the leading theme is financial security and peace of mind (404 mentions, 43.5%, with virtually no gender gap at 43.1% female to 44.8% male), voiced by a male client in Malawi who valued knowing "that there is a fallback plan in place" and rated the product 10 out of 10.

Men's dissatisfaction, by contrast, clusters around delivery and scope rather than comprehension: timely payouts account for 16.9% of male detractor comments versus 10.7% of female, and family coverage 10.7% versus 4.8%. A male client in Malawi asked that "our claim insurance requests should be processed on time rather than giving us false promises," while a male client in Uganda noted he had "never benefited" personally. Women's promoter comments, meanwhile, lean more heavily on health and medical coverage (42.9% versus 35.7% for men) and on simple processes and quick claims (11.2% versus 6.6%) — a female client in Kenya said simply, "It has really helped me in terms of my health cover-no more stress." Passive clients reinforce the experience-gap reading: 9.5% of passive comments cite having had no prior claim, and a female client in Malawi explained she would not give a 10 "because I haven't personally experienced a situation where I've needed to rely on insurance."

Three programming implications follow. First, women's higher NPS is an asset that is being partially forfeited: because their satisfaction rests disproportionately on health coverage and smooth claims, and their dissatisfaction disproportionately on explanation, targeted client education — delivered separately from the loan conversation, which several women flagged as crowding out insurance content — is the single highest-leverage intervention for lifting female advocacy further. Second, the gendered split in detractor themes argues against a one-size-fits-all service fix: turnaround time and family coverage should be prioritised for male clients, while comprehension and claims literacy should be prioritised for women. Third, the ten-point NPS deficit in disability-affected households, sitting alongside their elevated detractor share, warrants dedicated follow-up; it is a robust enough sample to act on but the survey does not tell us the mechanism, and accessible communication design is the obvious first hypothesis to test. As general context, disability- and gender-differentiated communication is a recognised priority in inclusive finance practice, but that framing is not a finding of this survey.
